{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=metrics+for+measuring+the+scientific+novelty+and+utility+of+research+questions&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.5040/9798892051286.0020\", \"title\": [\"Solutions to Chapter Questions\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.5040/9798892051286.0020\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.33140/jepr.04.02.02\", \"title\": [\"Measuring Social Media Attention of Scientific Research on COVID-19: An Investigation on Article-Level Metrics Data of Dimensions\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The purpose of this research was to evaluate the effectiveness of scientific productions on COVID-19 in social media for four months. This applied and scientometric study was conducted using the altmetrics approach. The data sources for this study included research papers published about the COVID-19 indexed in the Dimensions platform from December 2019 to March 2020. Approximately, 20% of the data on research articles with the highest citations in addition to 20% of the articles with the highest Altmetric Attention Scores (AASs) including title, journal, citation, and altmetrics indicators was extracted and analyzed by SPSS 16.0. The results showed that 1910 scientific productions about the COVID-19 were indexed in the Dimensions platform. A considerable number of these articles were accessible via preprint services and were published in journals such as The Lancet, JAMA, BMJ, and NEJM. Authors from China and Japan were the most active authors. All 382 articles had AAS, that is, all of these articles received attention, at least in one of the social media articles. The highest and lowest AAS for these articles ranged from 14030 to 6, respectively. These results showed a high rate of attention by researchers and users of social media to the articles presented on COVID-19. The results of this research also showed a significant positive relationship between citations and altmetric indicators. Based on the results, it was concluded that the information provided on COVID-19 was remarkably high. In addition, the result showed that the information demand by social media audiences was also high.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.33140/jepr.04.02.02\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2022, 5, 2]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7151807\", \"title\": [\"Measuring Local Power Outage Impacts with Utility–County Metrics, 2018–2025\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>National‑level studies in the United States usually examine power outages at broad units such as counties, utilities, or states. However, these broad summaries often hide where outages actually occur within a utility’s service area. We instead take a more granular approach by focusing on smaller units: the part of a utility’s service area within a single county.  We use this utility–county unit to measure severe outage impacts across the United States from 2018 to 2025 using 15 min EAGLE‑I data. This unit keeps both the utility’s responsibility and local geography visible in the analysis. To build these metrics, we reconstructed outage timelines, estimated annual customer counts, and identified severe events using a clear cutoff: at least 15\\\\% of customers or 30,000 customers affected. For each event, we calculated event count, duration, peak customers affected, total customer minutes interruption (CMI), and exposure per customer. Across the study period, we identified 191,160 severe events, resulting in 271.88 billion CMI. National totals varied sharply by year. For example, 2024 produced 70.06 billion CMI, whereas 2025 had a similar number of events but only 16.80 billion CMI. Most high‑CMI impacts occurred in a small number of utility–county areas, driven mainly by large peak impacts and long event durations rather than event count alone. The customer‑normalized metric also highlighted smaller or locally exposed areas absent from the absolute CMI rankings. This framework helps identify local outage hotspots and can support future analyses that link outage impacts with hazards, infrastructure conditions, or community vulnerability.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7151807\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.7717/peerjcs.392/table-1\", \"title\": [\"Table 1: Research questions and metrics.\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.7717/peerjcs.392/table-1\"}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "1bff85509b7d7e0ee3f6863f266f15e53f21f147484531ecb87cea6e7e3edc1d", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unassigned_problem", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.5040/9798892051286.0020", "doi:10.33140/jepr.04.02.02", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7151807", "doi:10.7717/peerjcs.392/table-1"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.5040/9798892051286.0020", "https://doi.org/10.33140/jepr.04.02.02", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7151807", "https://doi.org/10.7717/peerjcs.392/table-1"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
